title: Ὁπλισμὸς καὶ Ξάνθος
titleEn: The Arming and the Speaking Horse — Iliad 19.338–424
part: The Arming and the Speaking Horse (19.338–424)
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Achilles has refused food, and the old chiefs groan with him, each remembering his own home. Zeus pities him and tells Athena to put nectar and ambrosia into his chest, so that hunger does not come on him; she goes down like a bird of prey while the Achaeans arm. The host streams out from the ships, bright as flying snow, and Achilles arms himself with the gifts of Hephaestus, his eyes burning, unbearable grief in his heart and eagerness against the Trojans: greaves, breastplate, sword, shield, helmet, and last his father's spear, which only he can wield. Automedon and Alcimus yoke the horses, and Achilles calls on Xanthus and Balius to bring him back alive this time. Hera gives Xanthus a voice, and the horse bows his head and tells him that his day of destruction is near, that the blame lies with a great god and Fate, and that he is to be overpowered by a god and a man. The Erinyes stop the horse's voice. Achilles answers that he knows it well, and that he will not stop until he has driven the Trojans to their fill of war.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατο κλαίων, ἐπὶ δὲ στενάχοντο γέροντες,
μνησάμενοι τὰ ἕκαστος ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἔλειπον·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephato klaiōn, epi de stenachonto gerontes,
mnēsamenoi ta hekastos eni megaroisin eleipon·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, weeping, and in addition groaned the elders,
remembering what each in his halls had left;
sentences.i: So he spoke, weeping, and the elders groaned along with him, each remembering what he had left behind in his halls;
sentences.n: This takes up the scene of 19.303–337, where Achilles refused food and mourned Patroclus: the γέροντες ‘elders’ are the older chiefs who sit with him. ὣς ἔφατο ‘so he spoke’ is the stock close of a speech, and κλαίων is the present participle of κλαίω ‘weep’. ἐπὶ … στενάχοντο is ἐπεστενάχοντο split by tmesis, the imperfect middle of στενάχω ‘groan’, with ἐπί meaning ‘in addition, in sympathy’. μνησάμενοι is the aorist participle of μιμνῄσκομαι, ‘having remembered’; τά is the article used as a relative, ‘the things which’, and the imperfect ἔλειπον is put into English as ‘had left’ because the leaving came before the remembering.

sentences.t:
μυρομένους δ’ ἄρα τούς γε ἰδὼν ἐλέησε Κρονίων,
αἶψα δ’ Ἀθηναίην ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
myromenous d’ ara tous ge idōn eleēse Kroniōn,
aipsa d’ Athēnaiēn epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
Them lamenting, those same, seeing, pitied the son of Cronus,
and at once to Athena winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: The son of Cronus pitied them when he saw them lamenting, and at once he spoke winged words to Athena:
sentences.n: Κρονίων ‘son of Cronus’ is a patronymic standing for Zeus, who watches from Olympus. μυρομένους is the present participle of μύρομαι ‘weep, lament’, accusative plural, agreeing with τούς γε ‘those same’, the elders of line 338; ἰδών is the aorist participle of εἶδον ‘see’, and ἐλέησε the aorist of ἐλεέω ‘pity’. Line 341 is a stock introduction to speech, ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα ‘he spoke winged words’, with the imperfect προσηύδα of προσαυδάω. What follows is Zeus’ speech to Athena.

sentences.t: τέκνον ἐμόν, δὴ πάμπαν ἀποίχεαι ἀνδρὸς ἑῆος.
sentences.tr: teknon emon, dē pampan apoicheai andros heēos.
sentences.l: “My child, now altogether you have gone away from a man, a good one.
sentences.i: “My child, you have quite abandoned a good man.
sentences.n: The speaker is Zeus, and the words are for Athena. τέκνον ἐμόν ‘my child’ is an affectionate address. ἀποίχεαι is the 2nd singular of ἀποίχομαι ‘be gone from, leave’, here with the genitive, ‘you have gone away from’; πάμπαν ‘altogether’ strengthens it. ἀνδρὸς ἑῆος is ‘of a good man’: ἑῆος is the epic genitive of ἐύς ‘good’ (the form is sometimes taken instead as ἑός ‘one’s own’). The line is a reproach, not a question.

sentences.t: ἦ νύ τοι οὐκέτι πάγχυ μετὰ φρεσὶ μέμβλετ’ Ἀχιλλεύς;
sentences.tr: ē ny toi ouketi panchy meta phresi memblet’ Achilleus;
sentences.l: Truly now, is Achilles no longer at all a care to you in your wits?
sentences.i: Is Achilles no longer any concern of yours at all?
sentences.n: ἦ here marks a question, ‘truly?’, and νύ τοι is ‘now, then, to you’ (τοι = σοι, dative of the one concerned). μέμβλετ’ is the perfect μέμβλεται of μέλω ‘be a care’; the person who cares is in the dative τοι and the thing cared about, Ἀχιλλεύς, is the subject. οὐκέτι πάγχυ ‘no longer wholly’ is the strong form of ‘not at all’, and μετὰ φρεσί is ‘in the mind’. The English uses ‘concern’ for the verb and keeps the question.

sentences.t:
κεῖνος ὅ γε προπάροιθε νεῶν ὀρθοκραιράων
ἧσται ὀδυρόμενος ἕταρον φίλον· οἳ δὲ δὴ ἄλλοι
οἴχονται μετὰ δεῖπνον, ὃ δ’ ἄκμηνος καὶ ἄπαστος.
sentences.tr:
keinos ho ge proparoithe neōn orthokrairaōn
hēstai odyromenos hetaron philon· hoi de dē alloi
oichontai meta deipnon, ho d’ akmēnos kai apastos.
sentences.l:
That man in front of the straight-horned ships
sits lamenting his dear companion; and the others
have gone to their meal, but he is fasting and tasting nothing.
sentences.i: He sits in front of the straight-horned ships lamenting his dear companion; the others have all gone to their meal, but he goes fasting and tasting nothing.
sentences.n: κεῖνος ὅ γε ‘that man’ points at Achilles, sitting apart; ὅ γε is the article as a pronoun with the emphasising γε. νεῶν ὀρθοκραιράων is ‘the straight-horned ships’; what the ‘horns’ of a ship are is not known (the sense is traditional). ἧσται is the 3rd singular of ἧμαι ‘sit’, and ὀδυρόμενος the present participle of ὀδύρομαι ‘lament’; the ‘dear companion’ is Patroclus. οἴχονται is the present of οἴχομαι with perfect force, ‘have gone’, and μετὰ δεῖπνον means ‘after, to (their) meal’. ἄκμηνος ‘fasting’ and ἄπαστος ‘tasting nothing’ (+ genitive) are close in sense; ἄπαστος is a rare word, and its formation is not clear.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἴθι οἱ νέκτάρ τε καὶ ἀμβροσίην ἐρατεινὴν
στάξον ἐνὶ στήθεσσ’, ἵνα μή μιν λιμὸς ἵκηται.
sentences.tr:
all’ ithi hoi nektar te kai ambrosiēn erateinēn
staxon eni stēthess’, hina mē min limos hikētai.
sentences.l:
But go: for him nectar and lovely ambrosia
drip into his chest, so that hunger may not come upon him.”
sentences.i: But go, and drip nectar and lovely ambrosia into his chest for him, so that hunger may not come upon him.”
sentences.n: The command ἴθι ‘go!’ is the imperative of εἶμι; οἱ ‘for him’ is a dative of interest, and στάξον is the aorist imperative of στάζω ‘let fall in drops’, so Athena is to feed him without his eating. Nectar and ambrosia are the gods’ drink and food, and ἐρατεινήν ‘lovely’ is the stock epithet of ambrosia here. ἐνὶ στήθεσσ’ is ‘in the chest’ with elision, and ἵνα μή ‘so that not’ takes the aorist subjunctive ἵκηται (from ἱκνέομαι ‘come upon’, with μιν ‘him’), so the purpose clause reads ‘may not come’. This ends Zeus’ speech.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὄτρυνε πάρος μεμαυῖαν Ἀθήνην·
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn otryne paros memauian Athēnēn·
sentences.l: So having spoken, he urged on Athena, already eager;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and urged on Athena, who was already eager;
sentences.n: Line 349 is a stock line that also stands earlier in the poem (4.73) and keeps its English. ὣς εἰπών ‘having so spoken’ is an aorist participle, and ὄτρυνε the imperfect of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’. πάρος μεμαυῖαν describes Athena as ‘already eager’: μεμαυῖαν is the perfect participle, feminine accusative, of μέμονα ‘be eager’, and πάρος ‘before’ says that she was keen already, so Zeus only confirms what she wanted.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἅρπῃ ἐϊκυῖα τανυπτέρυγι λιγυφώνῳ
οὐρανοῦ ἐκκατεπᾶλτο δι’ αἰθέρος.
sentences.tr:
hē d’ harpēi eïkuia tanypterygi ligyphōnōi
ouranou ekkatepalto di’ aitheros.
sentences.l:
And she, to a bird of prey likened, long-winged, clear-voiced,
out of heaven leapt down through the upper air.
sentences.i: And she, like a long-winged, clear-voiced bird of prey, leapt down out of heaven through the upper air.
sentences.n: ἅρπη is a bird of prey; which bird is not known (the translation says only ‘bird of prey’). ἐϊκυῖα ‘likened to’ is the perfect participle of ἔοικα, feminine nominative, agreeing with ἣ ‘she’ and governing the dative ἅρπῃ; τανυπτέρυγι ‘long-winged’ and λιγυφώνῳ ‘clear-voiced’ are dative adjectives agreeing with ἅρπῃ. ἐκκατεπᾶλτο is the aorist of ἐκκαταπάλλομαι ‘leap down out of’; οὐρανοῦ is the genitive of the place she leaves, and δι’ αἰθέρος means ‘through the upper air’. The sentence ends mid-line 351.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὶ
αὐτίκα θωρήσσοντο κατὰ στρατόν·
sentences.tr:
autar Achaioi
autika thōrēssonto kata straton·
sentences.l:
but the Achaeans
at once were arming themselves throughout the host;
sentences.i: but the Achaeans at once were arming themselves throughout the army;
sentences.n: This begins in the middle of line 351. αὐτὰρ ‘but, and’ turns from heaven to earth, where the Achaeans prepare to fight. θωρήσσοντο is the imperfect middle of θωρήσσω ‘arm’, from θώρηξ ‘breastplate’, and κατὰ στρατόν means ‘through the host’. The army has been dismissed to eat (19.275ff), and now arms itself.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ Ἀχιλῆϊ
νέκταρ ἐνὶ στήθεσσι καὶ ἀμβροσίην ἐρατεινὴν
στάξ’, ἵνα μή μιν λιμὸς ἀτερπὴς γούναθ’ ἵκοιτο·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ Achilēï
nektar eni stēthessi kai ambrosiēn erateinēn
stax’, hina mē min limos aterpēs gounath’ hikoito·
sentences.i: and she dripped nectar and lovely ambrosia into the chest of Achilles, so that joyless hunger might not come upon his knees;
sentences.n: This begins in the middle of line 352; ἣ is Athena. Ἀχιλῆϊ is the dative of Ἀχιλλεύς with a single λ for the metre, and ἐνὶ στήθεσσι ‘in the chest’ is the same phrase as in 348. στάξ’ is the aorist 3rd singular ἔσταξε, with the augment and the final vowel lost, and so is not the imperative στάξον of 348: Zeus’ command is carried out, in almost the same words. The purpose clause has the optative ἵκοιτο (as the main verb is past), ‘might not come to’. λιμὸς ἀτερπής is ‘joyless hunger’, and the knees are named as the seat of a man’s strength.

sentences.t:
αὐτὴ δὲ πρὸς πατρὸς ἐρισθενέος πυκινὸν δῶ
ᾤχετο, τοὶ δ’ ἀπάνευθε νεῶν ἐχέοντο θοάων.
sentences.tr:
autē de pros patros eristheneos pykinon dō
ōicheto, toi d’ apaneuthe neōn echeonto thoaōn.
sentences.l:
and she herself, to the solid house of her father, great in strength,
went; and the others poured out apart from the swift ships.
sentences.i: and she herself went to the solid house of her father, great in strength; and the Achaeans poured out apart from the swift ships.
sentences.n: αὐτὴ δέ ‘and she herself’ contrasts Athena with Achilles. πρὸς … δῶ ‘to the house’ is a preposition with the accusative δῶ (= δῶμα), the two separated by πατρὸς ἐρισθενέος ‘of her father, great in strength’, that is Zeus. πυκινός is ‘solid’ of a house, as at Od. 7.81. ᾤχετο is the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘go’. τοί is the old article, ‘those’, here the Achaeans, and ἐχέοντο is the imperfect passive of χέω ‘pour’, so ‘they were streaming out’ from the camp; ἀπάνευθε νεῶν θοάων ‘apart from the swift ships’ shows where they went.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε ταρφειαὶ νιφάδες Διὸς ἐκποτέονται
ψυχραὶ ὑπὸ ῥιπῆς αἰθρηγενέος Βορέαο,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hote tarpheiai niphades Dios ekpoteontai
psychrai hypo rhipēs aithrēgeneos Boreao,
sentences.l:
And as when thick snowflakes of Zeus fly out,
cold, under the blast of the North Wind born of the clear air,
sentences.i: And as thick snowflakes of Zeus fly forth, cold, under the blast of the North Wind, born of the clear air,
sentences.n: This begins a long simile; its other half, ὣς τότε, is at 359. ὡς δ’ ὅτε ‘and as when’ is the stock opening, with the present ἐκποτέονται (epic for ἐκποτῶνται) ‘fly out, fly forth’, and ταρφειαὶ νιφάδες ‘thick snowflakes’ as its subject; Διός ‘of Zeus’ means they come from the sky. ψυχραί ‘cold’ agrees with νιφάδες. ῥιπῆς is the genitive ‘blast’ after ὑπό. αἰθρηγενέος Βορέαο is ‘of the North Wind, born of the clear air’: the sense of αἰθρηγενής is disputed (it may instead mean ‘bringing clear air’), and the form is epic genitive Βορέαο.

sentences.t:
ὣς τότε ταρφειαὶ κόρυθες λαμπρὸν γανόωσαι
νηῶν ἐκφορέοντο καὶ ἀσπίδες ὀμφαλόεσσαι
θώρηκές τε κραταιγύαλοι καὶ μείλινα δοῦρα.
sentences.tr:
hōs tote tarpheiai korythes lampron ganoōsai
nēōn ekphoreonto kai aspides omphaloessai
thōrēkes te krataigyaloi kai meilina doura.
sentences.l:
so then thick the helmets, brightly gleaming,
were carried out from the ships, and bossed shields,
and strong-hollowed breastplates, and ashen spears.
sentences.i: so then, thick and fast, gleaming brightly, the helmets were carried out from the ships, and the bossed shields, and the strong-hollowed breastplates, and the ashen spears.
sentences.n: ὣς τότε answers the ὡς δ’ ὅτε of 357: as thick as snow came the bronze. ταρφειαί ‘thick, close-packed’ is repeated from the snowflakes. γανόωσαι is the present participle of γανάω ‘gleam’, in epic uncontracted form. ἐκφορέοντο is the imperfect passive of ἐκφορέω ‘carry out’, with the genitive νηῶν for the ships they leave; ἀσπίδες ὀμφαλόεσσαι are ‘bossed shields’. κραταιγύαλοι means ‘with strong γύαλα’: γύαλον is the hollow or curved plate of a breastplate, and the compound is rendered by its parts. μείλινα is ‘of ash-wood’, from μελίη ‘ash’.

sentences.t:
αἴγλη δ’ οὐρανὸν ἷκε, γέλασσε δὲ πᾶσα περὶ χθὼν
χαλκοῦ ὑπὸ στεροπῆς·
sentences.tr:
aiglē d’ ouranon hike, gelasse de pasa peri chthōn
chalkou hypo steropēs·
sentences.l:
And brightness reached heaven, and all the earth round about laughed
under the gleam of bronze;
sentences.i: And the brightness reached heaven, and all the earth round about laughed at the gleam of bronze;
sentences.n: αἴγλη ‘brightness’ is the subject of ἷκε, a form of ἵκω ‘reach’, and οὐρανόν is the goal. γέλασσε is the aorist of γελάω ‘laugh’ with the epic doubled σ, and no augment; the earth ‘laughs’ because it shines, a poet’s figure rather than a sound. περὶ … χθών is ‘the earth round about’ with περί as an adverb. χαλκοῦ ὑπὸ στεροπῆς is ‘under the gleam of bronze’, the genitive στεροπῆς being a lightning-flash used of the glitter of weapons.

sentences.t:
ὑπὸ δὲ κτύπος ὄρνυτο ποσσὶν
ἀνδρῶν· ἐν δὲ μέσοισι κορύσσετο δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.tr:
hypo de ktypos ornyto possin
andrōn· en de mesoisi korysseto dios Achilleus.
sentences.l:
and beneath a din arose under the feet of men;
and in the midst of them armed himself heavenly Achilles.
sentences.i: and a din rose from beneath the feet of the men; and in the midst of them heavenly Achilles armed himself.
sentences.n: This begins in the middle of line 363. ὑπὸ δέ ‘and beneath’ opens the second thing the army does: the earth laughs above, and the ground rumbles under it. κτύπος is ‘din’, here the tramp of feet, and ὄρνυτο is the imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rise’. ἐν δὲ μέσοισι is ‘and in the middle’ with the dative plural μέσοισι (‘among them’), and κορύσσετο the imperfect middle of κορύσσω ‘arm’, from κόρυς ‘helmet’. Achilles’ arming now fills the scene.

sentences.t:
τοῦ καὶ ὀδόντων μὲν καναχὴ πέλε, τὼ δέ οἱ ὄσσε
λαμπέσθην ὡς εἴ τε πυρὸς σέλας,
sentences.tr:
tou kai odontōn men kanachē pele, tō de hoi osse
lampesthēn hōs ei te pyros selas,
sentences.l:
Of him there was a clang of teeth, and his two eyes
gleamed as if a gleam of fire,
sentences.i: His teeth gave a clang, and his two eyes blazed like the gleam of fire,
sentences.n: τοῦ ‘of him’ with ὀδόντων ‘of the teeth’ makes ‘his teeth’, and καναχή is a ‘clang’, a ringing sound, here made by the teeth. πέλε is the imperfect of πέλω ‘be’, without augment. τώ … ὄσσε is a dual, ‘his two eyes’, with the dual verb λαμπέσθην, which is the imperfect of λάμπομαι ‘shine’. ὡς εἴ τε is ‘as if’ or ‘like’, and σέλας is ‘flame, gleam’.

sentences.t:
ἐν δέ οἱ ἦτορ
δῦν’ ἄχος ἄτλητον·
sentences.tr:
en de hoi ētor
dyn’ achos atlēton·
sentences.l:
and into his heart
sank unbearable grief;
sentences.i: and unbearable grief sank into his heart;
sentences.n: This begins in the middle of line 366. ἐν … δῦν’ is the elided δῦνε, the imperfect of δύνω ‘sink into, enter’, split by tmesis from its prefix ἐν; its subject is ἄχος ‘grief’, and οἱ ἦτορ is ‘his heart’ (οἱ a dative of possession, ‘his’). ἄτλητον means ‘unbearable’ (from the root of τλῆναι ‘endure’). The grief is for Patroclus.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄρα Τρωσὶν μενεαίνων
δύσετο δῶρα θεοῦ, τά οἱ Ἥφαιστος κάμε τεύχων.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ara Trōsin meneainōn
dyseto dōra theou, ta hoi Hēphaistos kame teuchōn.
sentences.l:
and he, in eagerness against the Trojans,
put on the gifts of the god, which Hephaestus toiled to make for him.
sentences.i: and he, in his eagerness against the Trojans, put on the gifts of the god, which Hephaestus had toiled to make for him.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ἄρα is ‘and he’, the article as a pronoun. μενεαίνων is the present participle of μενεαίνω ‘be eager, strain’, with the dative Τρωσίν for the people it is aimed at: a fierce eagerness for a fight. δύσετο is the aorist middle of δύω ‘put on’, and δῶρα θεοῦ ‘the gifts of the god’ are the arms Hephaestus made (18.468 on) and Thetis brought (19.3–12). κάμε is the aorist of κάμνω ‘toil’, with the participle τεύχων ‘making’, so the arms cost the god labour.

sentences.t:
κνημῖδας μὲν πρῶτα περὶ κνήμῃσιν ἔθηκε
καλὰς ἀργυρέοισιν ἐπισφυρίοις ἀραρυίας·
sentences.tr:
knēmidas men prōta peri knēmēisin ethēke
kalas argyreoisin episphyriois araruias·
sentences.l:
Greaves first about his shins he set,
fine ones, with silver ankle-clasps fitted;
sentences.i: First he set fine greaves about his shins, fitted with silver ankle-clasps;
sentences.n: The arming, in the order a warrior used: greaves, breastplate, sword, shield, helmet. κνημῖδες ‘greaves’ are shin-guards. πρῶτα ‘first’ opens the list, and the aorist ἔθηκε ‘set’ is followed by περί ‘about’ with the dative κνήμῃσιν. ἐπισφυρίοις are the ‘ankle-clasps’ that held the greaves on. ἀραρυίας is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, feminine accusative plural, agreeing with κνημῖδας; καλάς ‘fine’ agrees with κνημῖδας as well. These two lines also stand at 3.330–331 and 11.17–18, and keep their English.

sentences.t: δεύτερον αὖ θώρηκα περὶ στήθεσσιν ἔδυνεν.
sentences.tr: deuteron au thōrēka peri stēthessin edynen.
sentences.l: Second, in turn, a breastplate about his chest he put on.
sentences.i: Second, he put on a breastplate about his chest.
sentences.n: δεύτερον ‘second’ continues the list, with αὖ ‘in turn’. θώρηκα is the breastplate, the accusative of θώρηξ, and ἔδυνεν is the imperfect of δύνω ‘put on’; περὶ στήθεσσιν is ‘about his chest’. The line also stands at 3.332, where the sentence goes on into a second line; here it stops at the end of the line.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ὤμοισιν βάλετο ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον
χάλκεον·
sentences.tr:
amphi d’ ar’ ōmoisin baleto xiphos argyroēlon
chalkeon·
sentences.l:
and about his shoulders he slung the silver-studded sword,
bronze;
sentences.i: and he slung about his shoulders the silver-studded sword, a bronze one;
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ὤμοισιν βάλετο is ‘and about his shoulders he slung’: ἀμφί is an adverb ‘about’ and βάλετο is the aorist middle of βάλλω ‘throw, sling’. ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον is ‘the silver-studded sword’, ἀργυρόηλον from ἀργυρός ‘silver’ and ἧλος ‘stud, nail’. χάλκεον ‘bronze’ stands in apposition to the sword, as at 3.334. The same words stand at 2.45 and 3.334.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα σάκος μέγα τε στιβαρόν τε
εἵλετο, τοῦ δ’ ἀπάνευθε σέλας γένετ’ ἠΰτε μήνης.
sentences.tr:
autar epeita sakos mega te stibaron te
heileto, tou d’ apaneuthe selas genet’ ēÿte mēnēs.
sentences.l:
but then the shield, great and stout, he took,
and apart from it a gleam came to be, as of the moon.
sentences.i: but then he took the shield, great and stout, and a gleam came apart from it, like the moon’s.
sentences.n: This begins in the middle of line 373. αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα is ‘but next’, and σάκος ‘shield’ is the object of εἵλετο, the aorist middle of αἱρέω ‘take’. μέγα τε στιβαρόν τε is ‘great and stout’ (στιβαρός ‘stout, strong’), a stock pair. τοῦ … ἀπάνευθε is ‘apart from it’, and γένετ’ is the aorist of γίγνομαι ‘came to be, arose’. ἠΰτε is ‘as’, and μήνης ‘of the moon’ is a genitive depending on σέλας understood (‘as the gleam of the moon’); ἠΰτε does not govern it.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἐκ πόντοιο σέλας ναύτῃσι φανήῃ
καιομένοιο πυρός, τό τε καίεται ὑψόθ’ ὄρεσφι
σταθμῷ ἐν οἰοπόλῳ·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ an ek pontoio selas nautēisi phanēēi
kaiomenoio pyros, to te kaietai hypsoth’ oresphi
stathmōi en oiopolōi·
sentences.i: And as when a gleam from burning fire appears to sailors out on the sea, a fire that burns high on the mountains in a lonely steading;
sentences.n: A second simile, for the shield’s gleam seen from afar; the second half is at 379. ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν … φανήῃ is ‘as when … may appear’: ἄν with the aorist subjunctive φανήῃ (an epic form of φανῇ) makes a general case, ‘whenever’. ναύτῃσι is the dative ‘to sailors’, and ἐκ πόντοιο ‘from the sea’ places the sailors out on the water, from which they see the light. καιομένοιο πυρός is ‘of a burning fire’, genitive of the thing the gleam belongs to, and τό is the article as a relative, ‘which’. ὑψόθ’ ὄρεσφι is ‘high on the mountains’ (ὄρεσφι with the old ending -φι). σταθμῷ ἐν οἰοπόλῳ is ‘in a lonely steading’; οἰοπόλος is usually glossed ‘lonely’, but this is not certain.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ οὐκ ἐθέλοντας ἄελλαι
πόντον ἐπ’ ἰχθυόεντα φίλων ἀπάνευθε φέρουσιν·
sentences.tr:
tous d’ ouk ethelontas aellai
ponton ep’ ichthyoenta philōn apaneuthe pherousin·
sentences.l:
and them, unwilling, blasts over the fish-teeming sea
apart from their dear ones carry;
sentences.i: while storms carry those sailors, against their will, over the fish-teeming sea, apart from their dear ones;
sentences.n: This begins in the middle of line 377. τοὺς δ’ οὐκ ἐθέλοντας is ‘and them not willing’, the sailors, accusative object of φέρουσιν ‘carry’ (present 3 pl.); ἄελλαι ‘blasts’ (‘storms’ in the free English) are sudden gusts or squalls. πόντον … ἰχθυόεντα is ‘the fish-teeming sea’, with the preposition ἐπ’ ‘over’ placed between the noun and its adjective. φίλων ἀπάνευθε is ‘apart from their dear ones’, ἀπάνευθε taking the genitive. The point of the comparison is the light seen across a dark sea by men blown away from home.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἀπ’ Ἀχιλλῆος σάκεος σέλας αἰθέρ’ ἵκανε
καλοῦ δαιδαλέου·
sentences.tr:
hōs ap’ Achillēos sakeos selas aither’ hikane
kalou daidaleou·
sentences.l:
so from the shield of Achilles the gleam reached the upper air,
the fine, wrought one;
sentences.i: so the gleam from the shield of Achilles reached the upper air, the fine and finely wrought shield;
sentences.n: ὣς … σέλας is the second half of the simile begun at 375. ἀπ’ Ἀχιλλῆος σάκεος is ‘from the shield of Achilles’ (Ἀχιλλῆος, the epic genitive), and αἰθέρ’ is the accusative of αἰθήρ ‘upper air’, the goal of ἵκανε, the imperfect of ἱκάνω ‘reach’. καλοῦ δαιδαλέου, genitives agreeing with σάκεος, mean ‘fine, finely wrought’: δαιδαλέος ‘wrought with skill’, as of the shield made by Hephaestus in book 18. The unit ends at the stop in the middle of 380; the rest of that line begins the next unit.

sentences.t:
περὶ δὲ τρυφάλειαν ἀείρας
κρατὶ θέτο βριαρήν·
sentences.tr:
peri de tryphaleian aeiras
krati theto briarēn·
sentences.l:
and lifting the helm, about his head he put
the weighty one;
sentences.i: and he lifted the helmet and set it on his head, the weighty helmet;
sentences.n: This begins in the middle of line 380. περὶ δὲ τρυφάλειαν ἀείρας is ‘and having lifted the helm’, with the aorist participle of ἀείρω ‘lift’; περί here goes with θέτο, ‘put around’ his head, and κρατί is the dative of κάρη ‘head’. τρυφάλεια is a word for the helmet, called ‘helm’ in the literal line and ‘helmet’ in the free one; its derivation is unknown. βριαρήν ‘weighty’ (from βρίθω ‘be heavy’) agrees with τρυφάλειαν.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἀστὴρ ὣς ἀπέλαμπεν
ἵππουρις τρυφάλεια,
sentences.tr:
hē d’ astēr hōs apelampen
hippouris tryphaleia,
sentences.l:
and it, like a star, shone forth,
the horse-tailed helm,
sentences.i: and it shone out like a star, the helmet with its horsetail plume,
sentences.n: This begins in the middle of line 381; ἣ is the helmet. ἀστὴρ ὣς ἀπέλαμπεν is ‘like a star it shone forth’, imperfect of ἀπολάμπω, with the comparison placed before the verb. ἵππουρις means ‘with a horse’s tail’, that is, with a plume of horsehair; it stands in apposition to τρυφάλεια. The star is the light of the helmet, not a particular star.

sentences.t:
περισσείοντο δ’ ἔθειραι
χρύσεαι, ἃς Ἥφαιστος ἵει λόφον ἀμφὶ θαμειάς.
sentences.tr:
perisseionto d’ etheirai
chryseai, has Hēphaistos hiei lophon amphi thameias.
sentences.l:
and shaken about were the plumes,
golden, which Hephaestus set around the crest, thick ones.
sentences.i: and the golden plumes shook all about it, which Hephaestus had set thickly around the crest.
sentences.n: This begins in the middle of line 382. περισσείοντο is the imperfect passive of περισσείω ‘shake about’, said of the ἔθειραι ‘plumes’ (the word means ‘hair’, here the horsehair streaming from the helmet). χρύσεαι is ‘golden’, the uncontracted form of χρυσαῖ. ἃς Ἥφαιστος ἵει is ‘which Hephaestus set’ (ἵει the imperfect of ἵημι, in the sense ‘let down, put’), λόφον ἀμφί ‘around the crest’ and θαμειάς ‘thick, crowded’, in the feminine accusative plural agreeing with ἃς.

sentences.t:
πειρήθη δ’ ἕο αὐτοῦ ἐν ἔντεσι δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς,
εἰ οἷ ἐφαρμόσσειε καὶ ἐντρέχοι ἀγλαὰ γυῖα·
sentences.tr:
peirēthē d’ heo autou en entesi dios Achilleus,
ei hoi epharmosseie kai entrechoi aglaa guia·
sentences.l:
And he made trial of himself in the gear, heavenly Achilles,
whether it fitted him and his splendid limbs ran freely in it;
sentences.i: Heavenly Achilles tried himself in the gear, to see whether it fitted him and whether his splendid limbs ran freely in it;
sentences.n: πειρήθη is the aorist passive form of πειράω ‘try, make trial of’, used with the genitive ἕο αὐτοῦ ‘of himself’ (ἕο = οὗ, the reflexive). ἐν ἔντεσι is ‘in the gear’, that is, in his arms. The indirect question εἰ … ἐφαρμόσσειε καὶ ἐντρέχοι has two optatives because the main verb is past: ἐφαρμόσσειε from ἐφαρμόζω ‘fit’ with οἷ ‘to him’, and ἐντρέχοι from ἐντρέχω ‘run in’, that is, ‘move freely’. ἀγλαὰ γυῖα are ‘splendid limbs’.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ εὖτε πτερὰ γίγνετ’, ἄειρε δὲ ποιμένα λαῶν.
sentences.tr: tōi d’ eute ptera gignet’, aeire de poimena laōn.
sentences.l: and to him it became like wings, and lifted the shepherd of the people.
sentences.i: and to him it became like wings, and lifted the shepherd of the people.
sentences.n: The subject, the armour, is understood from 384. τῷ is ‘to him’ (the article used as a pronoun). εὖτε is normally ‘when’, but here it is taken as introducing a comparison, ‘like’, and πτερά are ‘wings’. γίγνετ’ is the elided imperfect γίγνετο of γίγνομαι, ‘became’, and ἄειρε the imperfect of ἀείρω ‘lift’. ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is Achilles, the stock title of a leader. The armour lifts him instead of weighing him down.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ ἄρα σύριγγος πατρώϊον ἐσπάσατ’ ἔγχος
βριθὺ μέγα στιβαρόν·
sentences.tr:
ek d’ ara syringos patrōïon espasat’ enchos
brithy mega stibaron·
sentences.l:
And from the case he pulled out his father’s spear,
heavy, great, stout;
sentences.i: And he pulled his father’s spear out of its case, heavy, great and stout;
sentences.n: σύριγξ is a ‘tube’, and here it means the spear-case in which the spear was kept. ἐσπάσατ’ is the aorist middle of σπάω ‘pull out’, and πατρώϊον ἔγχος is ‘his father’s spear’, the spear of Peleus. The three adjectives βριθύ ‘heavy’, μέγα ‘great’, στιβαρόν ‘stout’ describe it, and the sentence goes on to say who can wield it.

sentences.t:
τὸ μὲν οὐ δύνατ’ ἄλλος Ἀχαιῶν
πάλλειν, ἀλλά μιν οἶος ἐπίστατο πῆλαι Ἀχιλλεύς,
Πηλιάδα μελίην, τὴν πατρὶ φίλῳ πόρε Χείρων
Πηλίου ἐκ κορυφῆς φόνον ἔμμεναι ἡρώεσσιν·
sentences.tr:
to men ou dynat’ allos Achaiōn
pallein, alla min oios epistato pēlai Achilleus,
Pēliada meliēn, tēn patri philōi pore Cheirōn
Pēliou ek koryphēs phonon emmenai hērōessin·
sentences.l:
this none other of the Achaeans was able
to swing, but Achilles alone knew how to swing it,
the Pelian ash-spear, which to his dear father Chiron gave
from the peak of Pelion, to be slaughter for heroes;
sentences.i: no other of the Achaeans was able to swing it, but Achilles alone knew how to swing it, the Pelian ash-spear that Chiron gave to his dear father from the peak of Pelion, to be the slaughter of heroes;
sentences.n: This begins in the middle of line 388, and the lines also stand at 16.141–144 (Patroclus, arming, does not take this spear), and keep that English. τὸ μέν ‘this one’ is the spear, and οὐ δύνατ’ ‘was not able’ is the imperfect of δύναμαι. ἐπίστατο ‘knew how’ takes the infinitive πῆλαι, an aorist of πάλλω ‘brandish’, and οἶος is ‘alone’. Πηλιάδα μελίην is ‘the Pelian ash-spear’, a spear of ash-wood from Mount Pelion, which the centaur Chiron gave to Peleus (φίλῳ πατρί). φόνον ἔμμεναι ἡρώεσσιν is ‘to be slaughter for heroes’, a purpose clause with the infinitive ἔμμεναι (= εἶναι).

sentences.t:
ἵππους δ’ Αὐτομέδων τε καὶ Ἄλκιμος ἀμφιέποντες
ζεύγνυον·
sentences.tr:
hippous d’ Automedōn te kai Alkimos amphiepontes
zeugnyon·
sentences.l:
And the horses Automedon and Alcimus, busying themselves about them,
were yoking;
sentences.i: Automedon and Alcimus busied themselves about the horses and yoked them;
sentences.n: Automedon and Alcimus are the two men who see to Achilles’ team. ἵππους is the object of ζεύγνυον, the imperfect of ζεύγνυμι ‘yoke’, and is put first for emphasis; ἀμφιέποντες is the present participle ‘busying themselves about’. The unit ends mid-line 393.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δὲ καλὰ λέπαδν’ ἕσαν, ἐν δὲ χαλινοὺς
γαμφηλῇς ἔβαλον, κατὰ δ’ ἡνία τεῖναν ὀπίσσω
κολλητὸν ποτὶ δίφρον.
sentences.tr:
amphi de kala lepadn’ hesan, en de chalinous
gamphēlēis ebalon, kata d’ hēnia teinan opissō
kollēton poti diphron.
sentences.l:
and around them they put the fine yoke-straps, and into the jaws
the bits they set, and the reins they drew tight backward
to the well-joined chariot.
sentences.i: They put the fine yoke-straps about the horses, set the bits in their jaws, and drew the reins back tight to the well-joined chariot.
sentences.n: This begins in the middle of line 393. ἀμφί is an adverb ‘about’, and λέπαδν’ are the ‘yoke-straps’, whose exact fitting is not clear. ἕσαν is the aorist 3rd plural of ἵημι ‘put, set’, and ἐν … ἔβαλον ‘put into’ shows tmesis, with γαμφηλῇς ‘the jaws’ in the dative; χαλινούς are the ‘bits’. κατὰ δ’ ἡνία τεῖναν ὀπίσσω is ‘and drew the reins back’, as at 3.261, the aorist of τείνω ‘stretch’. κολλητόν means ‘glued, well-joined’, as of fitted woodwork, and δίφρον is the chariot.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ μάστιγα φαεινὴν
χειρὶ λαβὼν ἀραρυῖαν ἐφ’ ἵπποιιν ἀνόρουσεν
Αὐτομέδων·
sentences.tr:
ho de mastiga phaeinēn
cheiri labōn araruian eph’ hippoiin anorousen
Automedōn·
sentences.i: And Automedon took the shining, well-fitted whip in his hand and sprang up behind the pair of horses;
sentences.n: This begins in the middle of line 395. ὃ δέ is ‘and he’, and the name Αὐτομέδων is held until the next line, so that the sentence ends with it. μάστιγα φαεινήν is ‘the shining whip’, with the perfect participle ἀραρυῖαν ‘fitted’ (as at 370). ἐφ’ ἵπποιιν is ‘upon the pair of horses’, the dual of ἵππος; he mounts the car those two draw, so the free English says ‘behind the pair of horses’. ἀνόρουσεν is the aorist of ἀνορούω ‘spring up’.

sentences.t:
ὄπιθεν δὲ κορυσσάμενος βῆ Ἀχιλλεὺς
τεύχεσι παμφαίνων ὥς τ’ ἠλέκτωρ Ὑπερίων,
sentences.tr:
opithen de koryssamenos bē Achilleus
teuchesi pamphainōn hōs t’ ēlektōr Hyperiōn,
sentences.l:
and behind, armed, went Achilles,
all-shining in his armour like the sun, Hyperion,
sentences.i: and behind him, armed, came Achilles, shining all over in his armour like the sun, Hyperion,
sentences.n: This begins in the middle of line 397. ὄπιθεν is ‘behind’, and κορυσσάμενος the aorist participle of κορύσσομαι ‘arm oneself’. βῆ is the aorist of βαίνω ‘go, step’; he takes his place behind Automedon. τεύχεσι παμφαίνων is ‘shining all over in his armour’. ἠλέκτωρ Ὑπερίων is ‘the sun, Hyperion’: ἠλέκτωρ is the usual word for ‘sun’ in this phrase, though its meaning is not certain (perhaps ‘the beaming one’), and Ὑπερίων is a name of the sun-god, ‘the one above’.

sentences.t: σμερδαλέον δ’ ἵπποισιν ἐκέκλετο πατρὸς ἑοῖο·
sentences.tr: smerdaleon d’ hippoisin ekekleto patros heoio·
sentences.l: and frightfully to the horses of his own father he called:
sentences.i: and he called out frightfully to his father’s horses:
sentences.n: σμερδαλέον is an adverb, ‘frightfully’, here of the voice in which Achilles calls. ἐκέκλετο is the aorist middle of κέλομαι ‘call, urge’, with the dative ἵπποισιν. πατρὸς ἑοῖο ‘of his own father’ shows that these are Peleus’ horses, the immortal horses. What follows is Achilles’ speech to the horses.

sentences.t:
Ξάνθέ τε καὶ Βαλίε τηλεκλυτὰ τέκνα Ποδάργης
ἄλλως δὴ φράζεσθε σαωσέμεν ἡνιοχῆα,
sentences.tr:
Xanthe te kai Balie tēleklyta tekna Podargēs
allōs dē phrazesthe saōsemen hēniochēa,
sentences.l:
“Xanthus and Balius, far-famed children of Podarge,
in another way, now, take thought to save your charioteer
sentences.i: “Xanthus and Balius, far-famed children of Podarge, take thought now in another way for the saving of your charioteer
sentences.n: Xanthus and Balius are the two immortal horses, and Podarge, a Harpy, was their mother. τηλεκλυτά is ‘far-famed’ and τέκνα ‘children’. The sentence runs on into 402–403. ἄλλως δή means ‘otherwise, now’, not the ‘idly, in vain’ that ἄλλως often has: think of some other way than the one that failed Patroclus. φράζεσθε is the present imperative middle of φράζομαι ‘consider’, with the infinitive σαωσέμεν (epic, from σαόω ‘save’) for what they are to see to. ἡνιοχῆα is the accusative of ἡνιοχεύς ‘charioteer’. Which man is meant, Automedon who holds the reins or Achilles who rides, is not said.

sentences.t:
ἂψ Δαναῶν ἐς ὅμιλον ἐπεί χ’ ἕωμεν πολέμοιο,
μηδ’ ὡς Πάτροκλον λίπετ’ αὐτόθι τεθνηῶτα.
sentences.tr:
aps Danaōn es homilon epei ch’ heōmen polemoio,
mēd’ hōs Patroklon lipet’ autothi tethnēōta.
sentences.l:
back into the throng of the Danaans, when we have had our fill of war,
and do not leave him as Patroclus, there, dead.”
sentences.i: back into the throng of the Danaans, when we have had our fill of war, and do not leave him there dead as you left Patroclus.”
sentences.n: ἂψ … ἐς ὅμιλον is ‘back into the throng’ of the Danaans, with ἐπεί χ’ ἕωμεν πολέμοιο, ‘when we have had our fill of war’: ἕωμεν is an aorist subjunctive of ἄω ‘satisfy’ (the usual explanation) with the genitive, and χ’ is κε. μηδ’ is ‘and not’, followed by λίπετ’, a 2nd plural aorist of λείπω used as a prohibition. The line is compressed: ‘do not leave [him] there dead, as [you left] Patroclus’, and τεθνηῶτα is the perfect participle of θνῄσκω ‘be dead’. This ends Achilles’ speech.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπὸ ζυγόφι προσέφη πόδας αἰόλος ἵππος
Ξάνθος,
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ar’ hypo zygophi prosephē podas aiolos hippos
Xanthos,
sentences.l:
Him then from under the yoke addressed the nimble-footed horse,
Xanthus,
sentences.i: Then from under the yoke the horse Xanthus, nimble of foot, spoke to him,
sentences.n: A new paragraph: the horse replies. τὸν δ’ ἄρα is ‘and him’, the object of προσέφη, the past tense of πρόσφημι ‘speak to’, and ὑπὸ ζυγόφι is ‘from under the yoke’, with the old ending -φι. πόδας αἰόλος is ‘nimble in his feet’, with πόδας an accusative of respect. αἰόλος is an epithet meaning ‘quick-moving’ (or ‘dappled’; the sense is not certain), and the horse is named at the start of the next line.

sentences.t:
ἄφαρ δ’ ἤμυσε καρήατι· πᾶσα δὲ χαίτη
ζεύγλης ἐξεριποῦσα παρὰ ζυγὸν οὖδας ἵκανεν·
sentences.tr:
aphar d’ ēmyse karēati· pasa de chaitē
zeuglēs exeripousa para zygon oudas hikanen·
sentences.l:
at once he bowed with his head; and all his mane
from the yoke-pad dropping down along the yoke reached the ground;
sentences.i: at once he bowed his head, and all his mane, dropping from the yoke-pad down along the yoke, reached the ground;
sentences.n: This begins in the middle of line 405. ἄφαρ is ‘at once’, and ἤμυσε is the aorist of ἠμύω ‘bow, droop’; καρήατι is the dative of κάρη ‘head’ (= Attic κεφαλῇ), so ‘with the head’. ζεύγλη is a part of the yoke-gear, probably a pad or loop; its exact fitting is not clear. ἐξεριποῦσα is the second aorist participle of ἐξερείπω ‘fall out of’, with the genitive ζεύγλης ‘from the yoke-pad’; παρὰ ζυγὸν is ‘along the yoke’, and οὖδας is the ground, the goal of ἵκανε ‘reached’.

sentences.t: αὐδήεντα δ’ ἔθηκε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη·
sentences.tr: audēenta d’ ethēke thea leukōlenos Hērē·
sentences.l: endowed with speech she made him, the goddess, white-armed Hera;
sentences.i: for the goddess, white-armed Hera, had given him a human voice;
sentences.n: The explanation of the miracle: a horse speaks only because Hera gives him a voice. αὐδήεντα ‘endowed with speech’ is from αὐδή ‘voice’, and the exact force of the word is debated; the translation follows the traditional ‘with a human voice’. ἔθηκε is the aorist of τίθημι ‘make’, with αὐδήεντα as the complement of an understood object ‘him’, and the gloss in English is a past perfect because the giving came before the speaking.

sentences.t: καὶ λίην σ’ ἔτι νῦν γε σαώσομεν ὄβριμ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ·
sentences.tr: kai liēn s’ eti nyn ge saōsomen obrim’ Achilleu·
sentences.l: “And truly, you, even now at least, we will save, mighty Achilles;
sentences.i: “Indeed, we shall save you even now, mighty Achilles;
sentences.n: Xanthus speaks. καὶ λίην is an intensifier, ‘and truly’, and ἔτι νῦν γε is ‘even now at least’. σαώσομεν is the future of σαόω ‘save’, 1st plural, so the horses promise to bring him out of this battle. ὄβριμ’ is the vocative of ὄβριμος ‘mighty’, said of Achilles, and Ἀχιλλεῦ is the vocative of Ἀχιλλεύς. The promise is made before the warning that follows.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά τοι ἐγγύθεν ἦμαρ ὀλέθριον· οὐδέ τοι ἡμεῖς
αἴτιοι, ἀλλὰ θεός τε μέγας καὶ Μοῖρα κραταιή.
sentences.tr:
alla toi engythen ēmar olethrion· oude toi hēmeis
aitioi, alla theos te megas kai Moira krataiē.
sentences.l:
but near for you is the day of destruction; nor are we
to blame, but a great god and strong Portion.
sentences.i: but your day of destruction is near; and it is not we who are to blame, but a great god and strong Fate.
sentences.n: The verb is not written in ἦμαρ ὀλέθριον (‘the day of destruction’, as at 19.294), so ‘is’ must be understood; τοι is σοι, ‘for you’. οὐδέ τοι ἡμεῖς αἴτιοι is ‘nor are we responsible’ (αἴτιοι ‘to blame’, nominative plural). θεός τε μέγας is ‘a great god’, who is only described at 413 and is Apollo; Μοῖρα ‘Portion’ is Fate personified, called κραταιή ‘strong’.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ γὰρ ἡμετέρῃ βραδυτῆτί τε νωχελίῃ τε
Τρῶες ἀπ’ ὤμοιιν Πατρόκλου τεύχε’ ἕλοντο·
sentences.tr:
oude gar hēmeterēi bradytēti te nōcheliēi te
Trōes ap’ ōmoiin Patroklou teuche’ helonto·
sentences.l:
For not by our slowness and sluggishness
the Trojans from the shoulders of Patroclus took the armour;
sentences.i: For it was not through our slowness or sluggishness that the Trojans took the armour from the shoulders of Patroclus;
sentences.n: οὐδὲ γάρ ‘for not’ gives the reason for the denial of blame. βραδυτῆτι ‘slowness’ and νωχελίῃ ‘sluggishness’ are datives of cause; ἡμετέρῃ ‘our’ agrees with the first and serves for both. ἀπ’ ὤμοιιν is ‘from the two shoulders’, with the old dual genitive, and τεύχε’ is τεύχεα ‘armour’, the object of ἕλοντο, the aorist middle of αἱρέω ‘take’. The armour is the arms of Achilles that Patroclus wore (16.130ff), and Hector took them (17.125ff).

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ θεῶν ὤριστος, ὃν ἠΰκομος τέκε Λητώ,
ἔκταν’ ἐνὶ προμάχοισι καὶ Ἕκτορι κῦδος ἔδωκε.
sentences.tr:
alla theōn ōristos, hon ēÿkomos teke Lētō,
ektan’ eni promachoisi kai Hektori kydos edōke.
sentences.l:
but of the gods the best, whom fine-haired Leto bore,
killed him among the front-fighters and gave glory to Hector;
sentences.i: but the best of the gods, whom fine-haired Leto bore, killed him among the foremost fighters and gave glory to Hector;
sentences.n: The ‘great god’ of 410 is named only by description: θεῶν ὤριστος ‘the best of the gods’, with ὤριστος the crasis of ὁ ἄριστος. ὃν ἠΰκομος τέκε Λητώ is ‘whom fine-haired Leto bore’; the god is Apollo. ἔκταν’ is the elided aorist ἔκτανε ‘killed’ (the Greek has no object), and ἐνὶ προμάχοισι is ‘among the front-fighters’; line 414 also stands at 18.456 and keeps that English. κῦδος is ‘glory’, the object of ἔδωκε.

sentences.t:
νῶϊ δὲ καί κεν ἅμα πνοιῇ Ζεφύροιο θέοιμεν,
ἥν περ ἐλαφροτάτην φάσ’ ἔμμεναι·
sentences.tr:
nōï de kai ken hama pnoiēi Zephyroio theoimen,
hēn per elaphrotatēn phas’ emmenai·
sentences.l:
And we two could run even with the blowing of the West Wind,
which they say is the lightest;
sentences.i: We two could run even with the breath of the West Wind, which they say is the lightest of winds;
sentences.n: νῶϊ is the dual ‘we two’, the two horses. καί κεν … θέοιμεν is the optative with κεν for a possibility, ‘we could run’, from θέω ‘run’. ἅμα takes the dative πνοιῇ ‘with the blowing’, and Ζεφύροιο is the epic genitive of Ζέφυρος, the West Wind, taken as the swiftest wind. ἥν περ ‘which indeed’ is the relative, picking up πνοιῇ, and ἐλαφροτάτην is the feminine accusative superlative of ἐλαφρός ‘light’, and φάσ’ is φασί ‘they say’; ἔμμεναι is the infinitive ‘to be’. The ‘lightest’ wind is the fastest; the Greek leaves ‘of winds’ unsaid.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σοὶ αὐτῷ
μόρσιμόν ἐστι θεῷ τε καὶ ἀνέρι ἶφι δαμῆναι.
sentences.tr:
alla soi autōi
morsimon esti theōi te kai aneri iphi damēnai.
sentences.l:
but for you yourself it is destined, by a god and a man,
to be overpowered by force.”
sentences.i: but you yourself are destined to be overpowered by force, by a god and a man.”
sentences.n: This begins in the middle of line 416. μόρσιμον ἐστι is ‘it is destined’, with σοὶ αὐτῷ ‘for you yourself’ in the dative, and δαμῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of δάμνημι ‘overpower’, so ‘to be overpowered’. θεῷ τε καὶ ἀνέρι are datives of the agent, ‘by a god and a man’, and ἶφι is ‘by force’. This ends Xanthus’ speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσαντος Ἐρινύες ἔσχεθον αὐδήν.
sentences.tr: hōs ara phōnēsantos Erinyes eschethon audēn.
sentences.l: So when he had thus spoken, the Erinyes held back his voice.
sentences.i: When he had spoken, the Erinyes checked his voice.
sentences.n: The Erinyes are avenging spirits; the poem gives no reason for their stopping the horse here. φωνήσαντος is a genitive absolute, the aorist participle of φωνέω ‘speak’, ‘when he had spoken’. ἔσχεθον is the aorist of ἔχω ‘hold’, in a longer epic form (= Attic ἔσχον), and αὐδήν is ‘voice’, so Xanthus is silenced.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ μέγ’ ὀχθήσας προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: ton de meg’ ochthēsas prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: Him, greatly vexed, addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: Greatly troubled, Achilles, swift of foot, said to him:
sentences.n: A reply formula: τὸν δὲ … προσέφη ‘and to him … said’, with the aorist participle ὀχθήσας ‘having been vexed’, from ὀχθέω, and μέγα ‘greatly’ as an adverb. πόδας ὠκύς is the stock epithet, ‘swift in feet’, and the line keeps the English of its other appearances (for example 16.48). Achilles answers the horse.

sentences.t: Ξάνθε τί μοι θάνατον μαντεύεαι; οὐδέ τί σε χρή.
sentences.tr: Xanthe ti moi thanaton manteueai; oude ti se chrē.
sentences.l: “Xanthus, why do you prophesy death to me? There is no need at all for you.
sentences.i: “Xanthus, why do you prophesy my death? There is no need for you at all.
sentences.n: Xanthus is the vocative Ξάνθε. μαντεύεαι is the 2nd singular present middle of μαντεύομαι ‘prophesy’, with the epic uncontracted ending (= μαντεύῃ), and μοι is ‘to me’. οὐδέ τί σε χρή is ‘nor at all is it necessary for you’: χρή ‘it is necessary’ takes the accusative σε, ‘you’, so ‘there is no need for you’. Achilles is annoyed, not surprised.

sentences.t:
εὖ νυ τὸ οἶδα καὶ αὐτὸς ὅ μοι μόρος ἐνθάδ’ ὀλέσθαι
νόσφι φίλου πατρὸς καὶ μητέρος·
sentences.tr:
eu ny to oida kai autos ho moi moros enthad’ olesthai
nosphi philou patros kai mēteros·
sentences.l:
Well I also myself know it, that my fate is here to perish,
apart from my dear father and mother;
sentences.i: I know it well myself, that it is my fate to perish here, far from my dear father and my mother;
sentences.n: εὖ νυ τὸ οἶδα is ‘well now I know this’, and καὶ αὐτός ‘even myself’. ὅ is the neuter relative used as ‘that’ (= ὅτι), and μόρος is ‘fate’, with ἐνθάδ’ ὀλέσθαι ‘to perish here’, the aorist infinitive middle of ὄλλυμι. νόσφι with the genitive means ‘apart from’; μητέρος is the epic genitive of μήτηρ, and φίλου ‘dear’ agrees with πατρός only; μητέρος has no adjective. Achilles knows he will die at Troy, far from his parents.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ ἔμπης
οὐ λήξω πρὶν Τρῶας ἅδην ἐλάσαι πολέμοιο.
sentences.tr:
alla kai empēs
ou lēxō prin Trōas hadēn elasai polemoio.
sentences.l:
but even so
I will not stop until I have driven the Trojans to their fill of war.”
sentences.i: but even so I will not stop until I have driven the Trojans to their fill of war.”
sentences.n: This begins in the middle of line 422. ἀλλὰ καὶ ἔμπης is ‘but even so, all the same’. οὐ λήξω is the future of λήγω ‘stop’, with πρίν ‘before’ and the aorist infinitive ἐλάσαι of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, so ‘until I have driven’. Τρῶας is its object, and ἅδην … πολέμοιο is ‘to their fill of war’, the adverb ἅδην taking the genitive. It is a bitter phrase, since the fill is the war’s killing. This ends Achilles’ speech.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα, καὶ ἐν πρώτοις ἰάχων ἔχε μώνυχας ἵππους.
sentences.tr: ē rha, kai en prōtois iachōn eche mōnychas hippous.
sentences.l: He spoke, and crying out among the foremost he held the solid-hoofed horses.
sentences.i: He spoke, and with a cry he drove the solid-hoofed horses on among the foremost fighters.
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα, καί ‘he spoke, and’ is a stock phrase, with ἦ the imperfect of ἠμί ‘say’. ἰάχων is the present participle of ἰάχω ‘cry out’, and ἐν πρώτοις is ‘among the first’, that is, in the front rank. ἔχε is the imperfect of ἔχω, ‘held’ in the literal line and ‘drove’ in the free one, with the horses going ahead, and μώνυχας ἵππους ‘solid-hoofed horses’ is the stock phrase for horses with an undivided hoof. Book 19 ends on Achilles’ cry as he goes into the fighting.
